summary:
Putrajaya is Malaysia's federal territory and administrative capital. It stands under the national framework: Malaysia criminalises same-sex conduct and gender nonconformity under the federal Penal Code 1936, and the territory's own Sharia code adds a second layer that reaches Muslims only.

Sections 377A and 377B of the federal Penal Code 1936 punish "carnal intercourse against the order of nature" and acts of "gross indecency" with up to 20 years' imprisonment and whipping. These provisions are not limited to Malaysian citizens and apply to visitors. Sodomy was first criminalised in 1871.

Putrajaya maintains its own Sharia code, which like the codes of the other federal territories and all 13 states typically criminalises same-sex activity and gender nonconformity through a ban on cross-dressing. These Sharia offences apply only to Muslims; non-Muslim visitors fall under the federal Penal Code alone. Penalties under such enactments elsewhere in Malaysia reach three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning, and enforcement is carried out by state Islamic religious departments. The enactments contain no legal definition of transgender dress, so the line between compliant and offending presentation is set by officers on the ground.

No legal gender-recognition procedure is recorded for Malaysia, and the Registration Department routinely rejects gender-marker changes. A 1982 National Fatwa Committee edict holds that sex is determined at birth and is unaffected by reassignment surgery; the edict was never gazetted and is not legally binding, but it is applied in practice, including to invalidate marriages involving transgender people. In August 2016 the Kuala Lumpur High Court ordered the National Registration Department to update a trans man's identity card, reasoning that Article 5(1) of the Federal Constitution guarantees a right to live with dignity in one's gender; that judgment was overturned on appeal in 2017.

Discrimination and violence against LGBT people are regularly reported across Malaysia, with transgender people particularly vulnerable. Enforcement documented since the 2018 election includes an October 2022 raid on a Queer Halloween party in Kuala Lumpur with at least 20 LGBT people arrested, an August 2022 raid on an LGBT venue with twenty men arrested, a Terengganu Sharia court ordering a lesbian couple caned, and November 2023 Johor plans for conversion-therapy centres. Government-run "rehabilitation" programmes had been attended by at least 1,733 people as of June 2021, based on interviews with 73 LGBT people across Malaysia between 2018 and 2021.

Malaysian law provides no protection against discrimination or hate crimes on grounds of gender identity or sexual orientation. Same-sex marriage and any form of partner recognition are unavailable. There is no explicit visa rule for transgender visitors; the nearest documented statement of entry policy is a 2001 declaration by then-Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad that Malaysia would deport any visiting foreign cabinet minister or diplomat who is gay.

No Putrajaya-specific enforcement case against a transgender or gender-nonconforming visitor or resident is documented in the sources reviewed. The national framework governs what a visitor faces in Putrajaya.
tangentialFactors:
Enforcement patterns elsewhere in Malaysia illustrate how the framework operates in practice: raids on social venues, arrests under section 377B, and Sharia proceedings against gender-nonconforming people. On 28 November 2025 police raided a male-only sauna in Chow Kit, Kuala Lumpur and arrested 208 men under section 377B, the largest such raid since 2022; a magistrate rejected the request to extend remand on the ground that no case had been made out, yet more than 130 detainees were still being held at one point, including 31 foreign nationals whose embassies intervened.

In July 2020 the Federal Territories Religious Affairs Minister announced that the Federal Territories Islamic Religious Department had his "full licence to carry out its enforcement actions" against transgender persons; the International Commission of Jurists demanded the order be revoked. Putrajaya falls within the federal territories framework alongside Kuala Lumpur and Labuan.

Violence against transgender women in Malaysia is lethal and largely unpunished: a trans woman was killed in Klang in June 2019, the third such killing of a trans woman in the country in fewer than two months. Arbitrary arrest of transgender people is documented over decades, including a mass arrest of 16 trans women at a wedding in June 2014 and a pattern of strip-searches and sexual assault by religious officials during detention.

Legal challenges have failed to remove the framework. The Federal Court struck down a Selangor cross-dressing provision in February 2021 and 16 Kelantan Sharia provisions in February 2024, but on federalism grounds about which legislature may enact the offence, not on the substance, and nothing under the federal Penal Code was decriminalised.
localsOnly:
Sharia offences for cross-dressing, liwat and musahaqah apply only to Muslim residents and are enforced by the relevant Islamic religious department; non-Muslim residents face only the federal Penal Code. Penalties under comparable Sharia enactments reach three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning, and sharia courts may commit women convicted of musahaqah to an approved home for up to six months or order offenders into counselling or rehabilitation in a religious institution for up to six months in some states.

Gender-marker changes on identity documents are routinely rejected by the Registration Department. The 1982 National Fatwa Committee edict on sex determined at birth was never gazetted and is not legally binding, but is applied in practice. The only successful documented marker change is historical: in 1975 the Registration Department recognised Sari Kartina binti Abdul Karim as female and the Johor Deputy Mufti permitted her to marry under Sharia law.

Government-run "rehabilitation" programmes had been attended by at least 1,733 people as of June 2021. In November 2023 Johor announced plans for conversion-therapy centres. No political party pursues LGBTQ legal reform, and Malaysian law provides no protection against discrimination or hate crimes on grounds of gender identity or sexual orientation.

No Putrajaya-specific enforcement case, arrest, or incident involving transgender or gender-nonconforming people is documented in the sources reviewed; the territory-specific picture rests on the existence of its Sharia code and the national framework. Whether Putrajaya's Sharia code contains a cross-dressing provision in the same terms as other states' enactments is not directly quoted in the sources, which describe the codes as typically containing such bans.

The sources do not state Putrajaya-specific penalties under its own Sharia code, nor whether the territory's Islamic religious department has conducted documented enforcement operations. Whether the 1982 fatwa is applied by Putrajaya authorities in practice is not separately sourced.

No explicit visa or entry rule targeting transgender visitors is recorded; the 2001 statement on deporting gay foreign ministers is the nearest documented entry-policy statement and its application to ordinary visitors is unresolved.
